type: frequency — the top of the scale; also duration (*I'll always remember*)
position: mid — after *be* and the first auxiliary, before the main verb; front only in commands (*Always lock the door*)
contrast: Position: *I always walk to work*, not *I walk always to work*; after *be* it follows the verb: *She is always late*. *Not always* is 'не всегда' (*He's not always right*); *always not* is wrong — say *never*. With a continuous tense it turns into a complaint: *He's always complaining* (вечно жалуется), not a neutral habit. 'Всегда' reaching up to now takes the present perfect: *I've always lived here*, not *I always live here since childhood*.

senses.gloss: At all times; on every occasion.
examples: She *always* takes the bus to work.
The store is *always* busy on Saturdays.
Do you *always* eat lunch at your desk?

senses.gloss: For all time, as far back as one remembers or into the future.
examples: I'll *always* remember that trip.
I've *always* wanted to see the Grand Canyon.
No matter what happens, we'll *always* be friends.

senses.gloss: Again and again, in an annoying way — with a continuous tense.
examples: He's *always* borrowing money and never paying it back.
Why are you *always* interrupting me?

senses.gloss: As a possible choice if nothing else works — usually with *can* or *could*.
examples: If you miss the bus, you can *always* call a cab.
We can *always* try again tomorrow.
Too expensive? Well, you could *always* rent one.

type: frequency — high on the scale, just below *always*
position: mid — after *be* and the first auxiliary, before the main verb; also front or end for emphasis
contrast: A habit that has stopped is *used to*, not *usually* + past: *I used to walk to school* (раньше ходил), while *I usually walked* only describes the typical case back then. 'Как обычно' is *as usual*, never *as usually*. Do not mix it up with *be used to* (привыкнуть): *I'm used to the noise*.

senses.gloss: In most cases; as a rule.
examples: I *usually* get up at seven.
Traffic is *usually* light on Sundays.
*Usually*, the meeting ends by noon.

position: mid — also front in the sense 'usually'; end in the sense 'in a normal way'
comparison: not gradable — in the sense 'usually'; *more normally* is possible in the sense 'in a normal way'
contrast: Russian *нормально* meaning 'fine, OK' is not *normally*: *How are you? — Fine* (or *OK*), not *Normally*; *Everything's fine*, not *Everything is normally*. In American English *normally* means 'обычно' far more often than 'нормально'.

senses.gloss: Usually; under ordinary conditions.
examples: I *normally* walk to work, but it's raining today.
The drive *normally* takes about an hour.
*Normally*, we'd be closed by now.

senses.gloss: In a normal way; as expected, with nothing wrong.
examples: The patient is breathing *normally* again.
Just act *normally* and nobody will notice.
Is the engine running *normally* now?

position: mid — before the main verb, after *be*; also front, especially in *generally speaking*
comparison: not gradable — *more generally* means 'in broader terms'
modifies: verbs, adjectives, participles and whole clauses
contrast: *Generally* is 'обычно' or 'в целом', not the emphatic 'вообще' of negatives and questions: *Я вообще не пью* is *I don't drink at all*; *А ты вообще кто?* is *Who are you, anyway?* The set phrase *generally speaking* is 'вообще говоря'.

senses.gloss: Usually; in most cases.
examples: I *generally* skip breakfast.
Flights are *generally* cheaper on Tuesdays.
The weather here is *generally* mild in the fall.

senses.gloss: By most people; widely.
examples: It is *generally* accepted that smoking causes cancer.
The new mayor is *generally* well liked.
The drug is not yet *generally* available.

senses.gloss: In broad terms, without going into details.
examples: *Generally* speaking, the reviews were positive.
She talked about the economy *generally*, not about any one company.

contrast: *Frequently* is more formal than *often*; the everyday question is *How often…?*, not *How frequently…?* It sits comfortably at the end: *It happens frequently*.

senses.gloss: Often; many times.
examples: He travels *frequently* for work.
Check the list of *frequently* asked questions first.
Buses run *more frequently* during rush hour.

position: mid — after *be* and the first auxiliary, before the main verb; also end, especially with *very*, *quite* or *too*
contrast: Position: *I often go there*, not *I go often there*; at the end it is most natural with a partner: *We don't eat out very often*. The t is normally silent (AW-fuhn), though AWF-tuhn is also heard. *Every so often* means 'время от времени' (not often), and *more often than not* means 'обычно'.

senses.gloss: Many times; in many cases.
examples: We *often* eat dinner on the porch in the summer.
How *often* do you go to the gym?
I wish we could visit *more often*.

type: frequency — the middle of the scale
position: any position — front, mid and end are all natural
contrast: Three different words: *sometimes* (иногда — *I sometimes work late*), *sometime* (когда-нибудь, в какой-то момент — *Let's have lunch sometime*) and *some time* (некоторое время — *It took some time*).

senses.gloss: On some occasions, but not always.
examples: *Sometimes* I just need a quiet day at home.
My sister *sometimes* works from home.
The subway gets really crowded *sometimes*.

contrast: It means 'now and then', not 'by chance': 'случайно' is *by chance* or *accidentally*. Spelled with double c and single s. It suggests fewer times than *sometimes* — roughly *once in a while*.

senses.gloss: Now and then; not often.
examples: We *occasionally* go out for Mexican food.
I run into him at the gym *occasionally*.
The trail is *occasionally* closed after heavy rain.

position: mid — after *be* and the first auxiliary; front only with inversion (*Seldom do we…*)
contrast: It is already negative, so no *not*: *I seldom go*, not *I don't seldom go*; the question tag is positive: *He seldom calls, does he?* Fronted for emphasis, it inverts: *Seldom have I seen such a mess*, not *Seldom I have seen*. In everyday American speech *rarely* or *not often* is more usual; *seldom* sounds formal or bookish.

senses.gloss: Not often; almost never.
examples: We *seldom* see snow this far south.
He *seldom* talks about his time in the Army.
*Seldom* have I heard such a moving speech.

position: mid — after *be* and the first auxiliary; front only with inversion (*Rarely does it…*)
contrast: Already negative, so no *not*: *I rarely eat meat*; the question tag is positive: *She rarely complains, does she?* Fronted, it inverts: *Rarely does it snow here*, not *Rarely it snows here*. *Rarely if ever* and *hardly ever* are standard; *rarely ever* is informal.

senses.gloss: Not often; hardly ever.
examples: I *rarely* watch TV anymore.
She is *rarely* late for work.
*Rarely* does a rookie play this well.

type: frequency — the bottom of the scale; also negative
position: mid — after *be* and the first auxiliary; front only with inversion (*Never have I…*) or in commands (*Never give up*)
contrast: English allows one negative: *I never eat meat*, not *I don't never eat meat* (Russian *никогда не* doubles it). Fronted, it inverts: *Never have I felt so tired*. For experience use the present perfect: *I've never been to Chicago*. In questions use *ever*: *Have you ever…?*, not *Have you never…?* unless you are surprised. Informal *I never took it* is about one occasion and means 'I didn't take it'.

senses.gloss: At no time; not once.
examples: I've *never* been to Alaska.
She *never* drinks coffee after lunch.
*Never* have I felt so welcome.

senses.gloss: Not, said with emphasis — often about a single occasion.
examples: He *never* even said goodbye.
I *never* touched your phone, I swear.
The package *never* arrived.

position: mid — after the subject in questions (*Have you ever…?*) and after the negative word (*nobody ever*); after its word after a superlative (*the best ever*); before its word in *ever higher* and *ever so*
modifies: verbs, superlatives, comparatives, *so* and whole clauses
contrast: Not in a plain affirmative statement: 'я когда-то был в Париже' is *I've been to Paris* or *I was once in Paris*, never *I have ever been to Paris*. Use it in questions (*Have you ever…?*), negatives (*nobody ever*, *hardly ever*), conditions (*if you ever…*) and after superlatives (*the best ever*). 'Как никогда' after a comparative is *than ever*: *I need you more than ever*, not *like never*. *Ever so* (*ever so slightly*) is informal and more British, but common in American writing. *Ever since* is 'с тех пор'; *forever* is written as one word in American English.

senses.gloss: At any time — in questions, negatives and conditions.
examples: Have you *ever* tried sushi?
Nobody *ever* calls the landline.
If you're *ever* in Denver, look us up.

senses.gloss: Of all time — after a superlative, after *first* or *only*, and in *than ever*.
senses.ru: когда-либо, за всю историю; как никогда
examples: This is the best pizza I've *ever* had.
She was the first woman *ever* to run the company.
Gas prices are higher than *ever* this summer.

senses.gloss: Always; all the time — in fixed phrases such as *ever since*, *ever after* and *as ever*.
examples: He's been sad *ever* since his dog died.
And they lived happily *ever* after.
She was, as *ever*, the last one to leave.

senses.gloss: More and more — before a comparative.
examples: Prices keep climbing to *ever* higher levels.
The suburbs are spreading *ever* farther from the city.

senses.gloss: Used for emphasis — in informal American exclamations with inversion, and after *how* or *why* in questions.
examples: Boy, was she *ever* mad!
Did we *ever* have fun at that concert!
How can I *ever* thank you?

senses.gloss: Very; in the smallest or gentlest way — in *ever so* before an adverb or adjective.
examples: She opened the door *ever* so slightly.
He lifted the sleeping baby *ever* so gently.

position: end — not mid (*The paper comes out daily*)
form: -ly from *day*; the same form as the adjective *daily*
contrast: The same spelling is an adjective (*a daily newspaper*) and a noun (*a daily* — ежедневная газета); only 'every day' after a verb is the adverb. Keep it at the end: *We exercise daily*, not *We daily exercise*. Also do not confuse the phrase *every day* (каждый день) with the adjective *everyday* (повседневный).

senses.gloss: Every day; once a day.
examples: The museum is open *daily* from 9 to 5.
Take this pill twice *daily* with food.
The list of volunteers is growing *daily*.

form: -ly from *week*; the same form as the adjective *weekly*
contrast: Also an adjective (*a weekly meeting*) and a noun (*a weekly* — еженедельник). *Biweekly* is ambiguous — it can mean twice a week or every two weeks — so Americans often say *every other week* to be clear.

senses.gloss: Once a week; every week.
examples: The team meets *weekly* to review progress.
The newsletter goes out *weekly*.
At this job we get paid *weekly*.

form: -ly from *month*; the same form as the adjective *monthly*
contrast: Also an adjective (*a monthly payment*) and a noun (*a monthly* — ежемесячный журнал). *Bimonthly* can mean twice a month or every two months; *every other month* avoids the doubt.

senses.gloss: Once a month; every month.
examples: Rent is due *monthly*, on the first.
The book club meets *monthly* at the library.
Interest on the account is paid *monthly*.

form: -ly from *quarter*; the same form as the adjective *quarterly*
contrast: It means every three months — a quarter of a year — not every quarter of an hour. Also an adjective (*quarterly earnings*) and a noun (*a quarterly* — ежеквартальный журнал).

senses.gloss: Once every three months.
examples: The company reports its earnings *quarterly*.
Freelancers pay estimated taxes *quarterly*.
The board meets *quarterly*.

contrast: Formal and financial; everyday speech says *every year* or *once a year*. *Biannually* means twice a year, *biennially* every two years. Spelled with double n and double l.

senses.gloss: Once a year; every year.
examples: The festival is held *annually* in June.
About two million people visit the park *annually*.
Salaries are reviewed *annually*.

form: -ly from *year*; the same form as the adjective *yearly*
contrast: The everyday counterpart of *annually*; also an adjective (*a yearly checkup*). The vowel is the one in *year* (YEER-lee), not the one in *early* (UR-lee).

senses.gloss: Once a year; every year.
examples: We see the dentist twice *yearly*.
The membership fee is paid *yearly*.
The town holds the parade *yearly* on the Fourth of July.

form: -ly from *hour*; the same form as the adjective *hourly*
contrast: The h is silent, so the adjective takes *an*: *an hourly bus*, *an hourly wage*. American *hourly* workers are paid by the hour, as opposed to *salaried* ones.

senses.gloss: Once an hour; every hour.
examples: Trains leave for the city *hourly*.
The nurse checks his temperature *hourly*.

senses.gloss: By the hour; for each hour worked.
examples: Most of the store staff are paid *hourly*.
Lawyers usually bill *hourly*.

form: -ly from *night*; the same form as the adjective *nightly*
contrast: It usually means every evening — shows and TV news run *nightly* — and never simply 'ночью': for that say *at night* (*Owls hunt at night*). Also an adjective (*the nightly news*).

senses.gloss: Every night or every evening.
examples: The show runs *nightly* at eight.
The kitchen is open *nightly* until eleven.
She checks the locks *nightly* before bed.

type: frequency — definite; also degree (*twice as big*)
position: end — before its word in *twice as … as*
form: *two* + old adverbial *-ce*, like *once*; the series goes *once*, *twice*, then *three times*
contrast: 'В два раза больше' is *twice as big (as)* or *twice the size (of)*; *two times bigger* is heard but criticized. Frequency takes no preposition: *twice a week*, not *twice in a week* (unless you mean 'within one week'). *Thrice* is archaic — say *three times*.

senses.gloss: Two times; on two occasions.
examples: I've been to Chicago *twice*.
Brush your teeth *twice* a day.
The phone rang *twice* and then stopped.

senses.gloss: Two times as much — in comparisons.
examples: Their house is *twice* as big as ours.
The repairs took *twice* as long as we planned.

position: end — mid in formal writing; front in *Again, …* and *Then again, …*
contrast: English *again* is neutral; Russian *опять* can sound annoyed, and English shows that with *yet again* or *Not again!* *What's his name again?* is not 'ещё раз' in the sense of doing something over — it means 'напомни, как его зовут'. 'Повторно' is *again* or *a second time*, not *repeatedly* (много раз). Most Americans say uh-GEN; uh-GAYN is also heard.

senses.gloss: One more time; once more.
examples: Could you say that *again*?
I failed the test, so I'll take it *again* in May.
Oh no, it's raining *again*.

senses.gloss: Back to an earlier place or condition.
examples: It's good to be home *again*.
She's feeling well *again* after the surgery.

senses.gloss: Used to ask for information that you were told but have forgotten.
examples: What was your name *again*?
Where are we meeting *again*?

senses.gloss: Used to repeat or stress a point already made.
examples: *Again*, I want to thank everyone for coming.
*Again*, the problem is money, not time.

senses.gloss: On the other hand — in *then again* and *but then again*.
examples: It's expensive. *Then again*, it'll last for years.
I might go. *But then again*, I might not.

contrast: *Constantly* (постоянно, всё время) is not *consistently* (неизменно, стабильно): *He's constantly late* means he is late all the time; *Her work is consistently good* means it is reliably good. With a continuous tense it signals irritation: *You're constantly checking your phone*.

senses.gloss: All the time, or so often that it seems like all the time.
examples: The baby cried *constantly* the first week.
Technology is *constantly* changing.
He's *constantly* checking his phone during dinner.

contrast: *Regularly* stresses a steady pattern, so it is not always *often*: *I see him regularly* suggests a routine (every Tuesday); *I see him often* just means many times. On American price tags *regularly* means 'at the usual price': *regularly $50, now $35*.

senses.gloss: Often and as a habit, or at fixed intervals.
examples: She exercises *regularly*.
Change your passwords *regularly*.
I wish the buses ran *more regularly* out here.

senses.gloss: Evenly; in an even pattern or rhythm.
examples: The fence posts are *regularly* spaced, ten feet apart.
His heart is beating *regularly* now.

senses.gloss: At the usual price — in American stores and ads.
examples: These jeans are *regularly* $60, now on sale for $40.
All *regularly* priced items are 20% off today.

contrast: *Repeatedly* means many times, not one more time: *I asked him again* (ещё раз) vs *I asked him repeatedly* (много раз). Russian *повторно* (a second time) is *again* or *a second time*.

senses.gloss: Many times; again and again.
examples: I *repeatedly* asked him to turn the music down.
The company had been warned *repeatedly*.
She pressed the button *repeatedly*, but nothing happened.

contrast: Careful writers split the pair: *continually* is 'again and again, with breaks' (*The phone rang continually*), *continuously* is 'with no break at all' (*The engine ran continuously for ten hours*). Everyday American usage also lets *continually* mean 'without stopping', so choose *continuously* when the absence of breaks matters.

senses.gloss: Again and again over a period of time, often annoyingly.
examples: He *continually* interrupts when other people are talking.
The office printer *continually* jams.

senses.gloss: Without stopping; all the time.
examples: The city's population has grown *continually* since 1950.
Our software is *continually* being improved.

contrast: Not the same as *continually*: *It rained continuously* means it never stopped; *It rained continually* means it kept raining on and off.

senses.gloss: Without a pause or break.
examples: It rained *continuously* for three days.
The machines run *continuously*, twenty-four hours a day.
She has lived in the same town *continuously* since birth.

senses.gloss: From time to time, often at more or less regular intervals.
examples: Check the tire pressure *periodically*.
The website is updated *periodically*.
He *periodically* glanced at the clock.

ru: как правило, регулярно, в обычном порядке
position: mid — before the main verb, after *be* and the first auxiliary
contrast: Russian *рутинно* sounds dull and mechanical; English *routinely* is neutral — 'as standard practice': *Newborns are routinely tested* means every newborn is tested as a matter of course. It can also mean 'so often that it is no longer surprising': *He routinely ignores my emails*.

senses.gloss: As a normal, regular part of a procedure or of life; as a matter of course.
senses.ru: как правило, регулярно, в обычном порядке
examples: Bags are *routinely* checked at the entrance.
Doctors *routinely* test newborns for hearing problems.
He *routinely* works sixty-hour weeks.

contrast: Not the same as *periodically*: *sporadically* stresses irregular, scattered occurrences with no pattern, while *periodically* suggests intervals.

senses.gloss: Now and then, irregularly and with no pattern.
examples: Fighting continued *sporadically* through the night.
He attended class only *sporadically*.
The Wi-Fi in this hotel works *sporadically* at best.

form: compound of *for* + *ever*, written as one word in American English
contrast: American English writes *forever* as one word in every sense; *for ever* is British. With a continuous tense it means 'constantly' and sounds annoyed: *He's forever losing his keys* (вечно теряет). *Take forever* is informal exaggeration, not literal. *For good* is a common informal synonym of 'навсегда'.

senses.gloss: For all future time; permanently.
examples: I wish this summer could last *forever*.
Once you post it online, it's there *forever*.
The accident changed their lives *forever*.

senses.gloss: For a very long time — an informal exaggeration.
examples: The line at the DMV took *forever*.
I've known her *forever*.

senses.gloss: Constantly; all the time — with a continuous tense.
examples: He's *forever* losing his glasses.
My neighbors are *forever* complaining about something.

position: mid or end — front in *Briefly, …* (in short)
contrast: *Briefly* is about length (ненадолго, кратко); *shortly* means 'soon' (вскоре): *I'll speak briefly* means the speech will be short, *I'll speak shortly* means it will start soon.

senses.gloss: For a short time.
examples: She *briefly* worked as a waitress in college.
The power went out *briefly* during the storm.
We stopped *briefly* in Memphis.

senses.gloss: In a few words; in short.
examples: Let me explain *briefly* how it works.
*Briefly*, the answer is no.
Could you put that *more briefly*?

contrast: It means 'with no end date fixed', not 'endlessly': a concert *postponed indefinitely* may still happen. 'Бесконечно' is *endlessly* or *infinitely*, and vague 'неопределённо' is *vaguely*.

senses.gloss: For a period of time with no fixed end.
examples: The concert has been postponed *indefinitely*.
You can't keep living with your parents *indefinitely*.
The plant will stay closed *indefinitely*.

contrast: US/UK split: in British English it means only 'for a moment'; in American English it very often means 'in a moment, very soon' — the flight attendant's *We'll be landing momentarily*. Context decides: past events and states (*was momentarily confused*) mean 'for a moment', future ones (*will be here momentarily*) mean 'soon'. American stress falls on the third syllable. False friend: Russian *моментально* (instantly) is *instantly* or *right away*, not *momentarily*.

senses.gloss: For a moment; very briefly.
examples: I was *momentarily* blinded by the headlights.
She paused *momentarily* before answering.

senses.gloss: In a moment; very soon — mainly American.
examples: The doctor will be with you *momentarily*.
We will be landing *momentarily*.

ru: за ночь, на ночь; в одночасье
form: compound of *over* + *night*; the same form as the adjective *overnight*
contrast: The adverb is stressed on *-night* (oh-vur-NYT); the adjective before a noun (*an overnight bag*, *an overnight success*) often moves the stress to the first syllable and belongs to the adjective dictionary. *Stay overnight* means 'остаться на ночь', not 'не спать всю ночь' (*stay up all night*).

senses.gloss: During the night, or for the whole night.
examples: Let the dough rise *overnight*.
Can I stay *overnight* at your place?
It snowed *overnight*, and the roads are icy.

senses.gloss: Very suddenly or quickly.
examples: The video made her famous *overnight*.
You won't learn a language *overnight*.

contrast: Russian *постоянно* meaning 'all the time' is *constantly* or *always*, not *permanently*: *He constantly calls me*, not *He permanently calls me*. *Permanently* is about lasting: *permanently closed* (закрыто навсегда), *live here permanently* (жить здесь постоянно).

senses.gloss: For all time; in a way that will not change or cannot be undone.
examples: The store is *permanently* closed.
The fire *permanently* damaged the old church.
Those files were *permanently* deleted.

senses.gloss: On a lasting basis rather than for a limited time — about where one lives or works.
examples: He's now *permanently* based in our Denver office.
She's *permanently* employed now, not on a contract.
Is he in town *permanently*, or just visiting?

form: -ly from *temporary*, with y changed to i
contrast: American stress falls on the third syllable (tem-puh-RAIR-uh-lee); British English often stresses the first. Do not confuse it with *temporally* (во времени, 'relating to time').

senses.gloss: For a limited time; not permanently.
examples: The road is *temporarily* closed for repairs.
I'm *temporarily* staying with my brother.
The website is *temporarily* unavailable.
